title: Rise and recline chairs for arthritis and frailty (UK)
meta_title: Rise and Recline Chairs for Arthritis: Are They Right?
meta_description: Whether a rise and recline chair could help with arthritis and frailty, what to check before buying, the risks, and how to get advice from an occupational therapist.

direct_answer: A rise and recline chair tilts forward to help you stand and can recline for comfort. It can help some people with arthritis and frailty, but it may also reduce leg strength if it does all the work. Ask an occupational therapist for advice on size and features before buying.

content:
A rise and recline chair has a motor that tilts the seat forward and up to help you stand, and reclines for resting. If arthritis and frailty make getting out of a chair hard, it can seem like the answer. It can help, but it is a big purchase and not right for everyone.

This guide covers the pros and cons, what to check, and where to get advice. It is educational information, not a product recommendation.

Potential benefits

  • Less strain on painful hips and knees when standing.
  • A safer rise if you are unsteady.
  • Easy reclining to raise your legs or rest.

Things to consider

  • If the chair does all the lifting, your leg muscles may weaken. Try using it partly, then pushing up yourself.
  • Standing up from other chairs, toilets and cars may become harder if you only use this chair.
  • Reclining for long periods can increase stiffness and pressure on the skin.
  • Make sure you can operate the controls with painful hands.

What to check before buying

  • Seat height and depth suit your body: your feet should be flat on the floor and the back of your knees should not press on the seat edge.
  • Seat width with room to move, and firm armrests.
  • Single or dual motor (dual lets the back and legs move separately).
  • Battery backup in case of a power cut.
  • A home trial and a clear returns policy.

Get advice first

An occupational therapist can assess you and recommend whether a riser recliner, chair raisers or a different chair would suit you better. Ask your GP or council for a referral. Chair raisers or a higher, firm chair are often a simpler, cheaper option.

Cost and VAT

Riser recliners are usually bought privately. If you have a long-term condition, you may not have to pay VAT on equipment designed for disabled people. Ask the supplier about VAT relief.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Will the NHS or council pay for one?

Usually not, but they may provide chair raisers or other equipment after an assessment.

Can I sleep in it?

Some people do for short periods, but sleeping in a chair long term can cause stiffness, leg swelling and skin problems.

Should I buy second-hand?

It can save money, but check the motor, controls and fit, and get advice on whether it suits you.
